content: Voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) programs are responsible for providing a range of health services, including HIV testing, family planning (such as condom distribution), sexually transmitted infection (STI) testing and treatment, and general health services. Surveys conducted across eight countries indicate that VMMC is considered acceptable by 40–85% of men and 50–93% of women. The cost of performing VMMC varies significantly across countries and settings, with key cost factors being personnel and consumables. Eleven studies have reported the cost per VMMC procedure, with estimates ranging from $23 to $191 in various African countries. Larger studies with better generalizability reported costs between $66 and $160 per procedure. In four sub-Saharan African countries, lower unit costs were associated with factors such as providing services in primary healthcare facilities rather than hospitals, integrating VMMC with other services (e.g., antiretroviral therapy [ART] and prevention of mother-to-child transmission [PMTCT]), higher procedure volumes, and delegating tasks to less specialized staff. Conversely, higher costs were observed in facilities conducting outreach or employing more experienced healthcare workers. Across all four countries, staff costs were the largest component of VMMC unit costs, followed by consumables like circumcision kits and HIV test kits. Task-shifting from physicians to clinical officers in mobile camps and fixed centers contributed to cost savings. Training Ugandan surgeons inexperienced in adult circumcision also improved efficiency and reduced costs. The authors of the four-country study suggest that quality VMMC services can be delivered at lower costs by optimizing service delivery during peak demand seasons, integrating other HIV services, and adjusting staffing models. VMMC has been shown to be cost-effective, as evidenced by nine studies conducted in East and Southern Africa. The cost per HIV infection averted in adults ranged from $117 in Kenya to $4,949 in Rwanda, with other countries falling within this range. The cost-effectiveness was greatest for longer projected time periods post-circumcision, as more heterosexual acts are partially protected. A 2016 UNAIDS and WHO consultation concluded that VMMC is most cost-effective when performed on males aged 15–29, as fewer circumcisions are needed to prevent one HIV infection, and net savings are highest. A study in Zimbabwe estimated savings of $55–198 million in ART costs from 2017 to 2030 due to the preventive effects of VMMC. The World Bank’s 2015 Disease Control Priorities listed VMMC as one of 44 essential surgical procedures due to its cost-effectiveness and wide applicability. Ethical considerations emphasize the importance of informed consent, human rights, and safety in VMMC programs. The 2007 WHO/UNAIDS recommendations remain relevant, advocating for voluntary procedures based on accurate information and without coercion or discrimination. VMMC should complement, not replace, other HIV prevention strategies. Stakeholders must be consulted to justify the promotion of VMMC, and individuals who decline the procedure should not face stigma or discrimination. Informed consent is a core human right, requiring adequate information and the ability to withdraw consent at any time without prejudice. Countries lacking explicit legal references to informed consent may infer this right from broader principles like privacy, dignity, and bodily integrity. Public health justifications for VMMC depend on reliable scientific data and ethical implementation. VMMC should always be part of a comprehensive HIV prevention package and not replace other methods. Equity in access to VMMC services is crucial, with efforts to reduce barriers such as costs, follow-up care, and travel. Traditional community values and social factors influence the acceptability of VMMC and, indirectly, equity. Feasibility studies have demonstrated the scalability of VMMC, with nearly 23 million men and boys circumcised by the end of 2018. However, challenges remain in achieving greater coverage, particularly among adult males at higher risk of HIV infection. Integrated approaches, combining VMMC with routine services, have shown benefits such as strengthened local ownership and partnerships, despite slower initial scale-up. VMMC programs should also address harmful gender norms and gender-based violence while minimizing potential negative impacts, such as risk compensation or mischaracterization of the procedure’s benefits. Clear communication is essential in VMMC programs. Men with HIV should be virally suppressed on ART before undergoing circumcision to reduce transmission risks during the healing period. Messages should be culturally sensitive, tailored to local contexts, and emphasize the differences between male circumcision and female genital mutilation, which has no medical benefits and causes significant harm. Studies should also evaluate the feasibility and cost-effectiveness of integrating other health services with VMMC. For younger adolescents (ages 10–14), offering VMMC requires careful consideration of public health burden, informed consent, safety, and feasibility. Adolescents’ capacity to provide informed consent varies, and non-emergency procedures should be postponed until the individual is sufficiently mature. Safety must be prioritized, as younger adolescents may face a slightly higher risk of rare adverse events. Physical maturity is a key factor in the safety of VMMC for younger adolescents, and procedures should be deferred for those with immature genitalia. Policymakers must consider adolescents’ and communities’ preferences, including the choice of formal healthcare providers over traditional practitioners. While VMMC for younger adolescents was not initially prioritized, uptake among this group has increased in recent years, particularly as adult coverage levels have risen. Sustaining effective HIV prevention coverage requires reorienting services to uncircumcised cohorts, but evidence on the optimal age range for VMMC remains limited.
